description:
**The two state-machine ports are only as aligned as review has made them.** `README.md` names this as the next thing worth doing, and it is right: two hand-ported implementations of a 27-row transition table WILL drift, and drift here is invisible until a user's upload behaves differently on one platform.

`docs/reference/state-machine.md` is the source of truth — §1 states, §2 the 27-row transition table, §3 events, §4 invariants, §5 recovery-as-a-transition, §6 cancelation of a job the app has never seen running. §5 and §6 are the subtle ones and the most likely to diverge.

`unblock`: it ships nothing a user sees. It is what makes every later change to either port safe, which is why it comes before the stubs are filled rather than after.

userStories.title: A shared, language-neutral vector set derived from the spec
userStories.description: One file both ports read. Not two test suites that happen to agree.
acceptanceCriteria: Vectors live in a language-neutral format in the repository, readable by both Swift and Kotlin.
Every one of the 27 transition-table rows is covered by at least one vector.
§4's invariants, §5's recovery transitions and §6's cancel-a-job-never-seen-running case each have explicit vectors.
Each vector cites the spec section it encodes, so a spec change has a findable blast radius.

userStories.title: Both ports run the vectors, and a divergence fails the build
userStories.description: The point is not that vectors exist. The point is that drift becomes a red build.
acceptanceCriteria: The Swift port runs the full vector set in `swift test`.
The Kotlin port runs the same set in its Gradle test task.
A deliberately introduced divergence in ONE port fails that port's suite — demonstrated, not asserted.
